heading: Listed and visible are different things
candidates.text: Separate "listed" from "visible in a normal broad search." Marketplace search is not a complete inventory dump. It limits result sets, ranks and groups similar offers, tries to avoid race conditions, and usually shows the best matches first. Search can be affected by ranking, grouping, filters, verification state, offer state, rental state, reliability, price, supply and demand, or machine errors.

heading: Check the machine directly
candidates.text: Start in the Machines page for the host account. Confirm that the machine is online, listed, has active offers, has no red machine errors, and is not currently rented in a way that hides the offer you expect to see. Also confirm required details such as direct ports, RAM, upload speed, and download speed are populated, and that reliability is above the relevant gate.

heading: Introduction
candidates.text: Understand reliability score, uptime expectations, common score drops, and practical recovery steps.

heading: Why does reliability drop after rentals, reboots, or disconnects?
candidates.text: Reliability can drop when the platform observes instability, failed starts, disconnections, downtime, network failures, driver or GPU failures, thermal or power events, or active rental disruption. Short rentals can expose startup and runtime failures quickly. Reboots or disconnects during active commitments can hurt reliability.

heading: How quickly does reliability recover?
candidates.text: Reliability recovery depends on sustained stable operation and the machine's recent incident history. Some error messages can clear after the underlying issue is resolved, but reliability score recovery should not be treated as an instant reset. Keep the machine stable and error-free, then monitor the score over time.

heading: What should I do when reliability is at or below 0.9?
candidates.text: Reliability greater than 0.9 is a self-test and verification gate. If the machine is at or below the threshold, the normal self-test can fail before renting the temporary instance and the machine will not enter the verification pool. Keep the machine stable, resolve recent hardware, network, driver, daemon, thermal, power, or rental-disruption issues, then retry once the score recovers.

heading: What should I do when reliability is at or below 0.9?
candidates.text: The gate exists so machines that have not been online for a sufficient amount of time are not put through verification testing. Above the gate, higher reliability can make verification more likely because the automated process has more confidence in the machine. Sustained instability after verification can cause a verified machine to be deverified.

heading: Will restarting lower reliability or remove verification?
candidates.text: Reliability does not directly determine verification state by itself. Verification is separate from the reliability score, but outages, failed starts, driver issues, network drops, or other instability can reduce reliability and may eventually contribute to deverification if the machine becomes unhealthy. Plan restarts around active contracts and use maintenance windows whenever possible.

candidates.text: | **Machine reported by renter** | A renter filed a problem report against one of your machines. Reports are often the earliest sign something is wrong — fix the issue before it affects your reliability score or rentals. |

heading: Before Maintenance
candidates.text: A single machine can have multiple active rental contracts from different clients. Do not take the machine offline until every active rental contract has ended.

heading: Planned Maintenance
candidates.text: For planned work, set the offer end date to the maintenance date so new rentals do not run past your planned downtime. Existing contracts keep their accepted end date, so choose a date that still honors the latest active rental.

heading: How do I unlist, delete, or recreate a machine?
candidates.text: Unlisting stops new rental contracts from being created, but it does not end existing contracts. Deleting or recreating a machine should only happen after active commitments and stored workloads are understood. Recreating may be useful after a failed install, stale record, or major hardware change, but do not use undocumented reset or recovery flags unless Vast support specifically instructs you to do so.
